misconceptions.statement: All germs are bacteria.
misconceptions.why: Everyday talk uses 'bacteria' and 'germs' as the same word.
misconceptions.fix: Germs include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa. These are different kinds of microorganisms.

probe.question: Is a virus that causes flu a bacterium?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all germs are bacteria.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar word covers the whole category
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about microbes and disease

misconceptions.statement: All germs are harmful and should be killed.
misconceptions.why: Advertisements show germs as enemies everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: Most microbes are harmless or useful, like those that make curd or help digestion. Only a few cause disease.

probe.question: Are the bacteria that turn milk into curd harmful?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all bacteria are harmful.

misconceptions.root_belief: a whole group is bad because some members are
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about microorganisms

misconceptions.statement: If hands look clean, they have no germs.
misconceptions.why: Students trust what they can see.
misconceptions.fix: Germs are far too small to see, so clean-looking hands can carry many. Washing with soap is still needed.

probe.question: Hands look spotless. Do they need washing before eating?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is no dirt so no germs.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on children's reasoning about invisible microbes

misconceptions.statement: Germs spread only through dirty or smelly things.
misconceptions.why: Dirt and bad smell are linked with disease in everyday talk.
misconceptions.fix: Germs can be on clean-looking things such as door handles, phones and hands. Touching them then your face or food spreads germs.

probe.question: Can a shiny, clean-looking door handle spread germs?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only dirty things have germs.

misconceptions.root_belief: appearance shows whether something is safe

misconceptions.statement: Germs spread only when a sick person touches you.
misconceptions.why: Contact is the most obvious route to students.
misconceptions.fix: Some germs travel in tiny droplets from coughs, sneezes and talking, so you can catch them without touching.

probe.question: A sick classmate sneezes 1 metre away without touching you. Can you get infected?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there was no touch.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: You catch a cold from being out in cold weather or getting wet.
misconceptions.why: The word 'cold' and common advice from elders link weather with illness.
misconceptions.fix: Colds are caused by viruses spread from infected people. Cold weather itself does not cause them.

probe.question: What causes a common cold?
probe.wrong_answer: Cold air and getting wet in rain.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of lay beliefs about colds and flu

misconceptions.statement: Diseases like malaria and dengue spread from sick people by touch or air.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all diseases spread person to person directly.
misconceptions.fix: Malaria and dengue spread through mosquito bites, which carry the germ from one person to another.

probe.question: How does malaria spread?
probe.wrong_answer: By touching or breathing near a malaria patient.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Soap works by killing all germs on the skin immediately.
misconceptions.why: Soap advertisements say 'kills 99.9% germs'.
misconceptions.fix: Soap mainly loosens germs and dirt from skin so water washes them off. Rubbing and rinsing do most of the work.

probe.question: Why must you rinse hands after soaping?
probe.wrong_answer: No need; soap already killed everything.

misconceptions.root_belief: products work by magic instantly

misconceptions.statement: Only antibacterial or liquid soap works; plain soap does not.
misconceptions.why: Marketing suggests special soaps are stronger.
misconceptions.fix: Plain soap and water remove germs well when used properly. Special antibacterial soaps are not needed for daily handwashing.

probe.question: Is plain bar soap enough to clean hands properly?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only antibacterial soap works.

misconceptions.root_belief: costlier or special product works better

misconceptions.statement: Rinsing hands with water alone is as good as using soap.
misconceptions.why: Wet hands look clean and feel clean.
misconceptions.fix: Water alone cannot lift greasy dirt and germs well. Soap breaks the grip of grease so germs wash away.

probe.question: Is a quick rinse under a tap enough before lunch?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, water washes germs away just as well.

misconceptions.root_belief: what looks clean is clean

misconceptions.statement: Wetting hands and a quick soap rub of 5 seconds is enough.
misconceptions.why: Students think the soap itself acts instantly.
misconceptions.fix: Rub with soap for at least 20 seconds so germs are loosened and removed.

probe.question: How long should you scrub hands with soap?
probe.wrong_answer: About 5 seconds.

misconceptions.root_belief: a small amount gives the full effect

misconceptions.statement: Washing only the palms is enough to clean hands.
misconceptions.why: Palms are what students see touching things most.
misconceptions.fix: Germs hide on backs of hands, between fingers, under nails and around thumbs. All these must be scrubbed.

probe.question: Which parts of the hand need scrubbing?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the palms.

misconceptions.root_belief: the obvious part is the whole thing

misconceptions.statement: Hands need washing only when they look dirty.
misconceptions.why: Washing is linked to visible mess.
misconceptions.fix: Wash before eating or cooking and after using the toilet, coughing or touching animals, even when hands look clean.

probe.question: After using the toilet, hands look clean. Should you wash?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are clean.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Coughing into your bare palm is fine if you wipe it later.
misconceptions.why: Palm is the natural reflex to cover the mouth.
misconceptions.fix: Cough into your bent elbow or a tissue, because germs on palms spread to everything you touch.

probe.question: Best way to cover a sneeze?
probe.wrong_answer: Cover with the palm of the hand.

misconceptions.root_belief: covering anything is enough

misconceptions.statement: Wearing a mask or covering the mouth is only for sick people.
misconceptions.why: Masks are linked to patients.
misconceptions.fix: Sick people should cover coughs, and masks can also protect healthy people in crowded or risky places.

probe.question: Can a healthy person benefit from a mask near a coughing patient?
probe.wrong_answer: No, masks are only for the sick.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule for one group applies to only that group

misconceptions.statement: Boiling water for a few seconds as it warms makes it safe.
misconceptions.why: Students think any heating kills germs.
misconceptions.fix: Water should reach a rolling boil and continue for about a minute. Then let it cool in a covered container.

probe.question: How long should drinking water boil?
probe.wrong_answer: Until bubbles first appear.

misconceptions.root_belief: a small amount gives the full effect

misconceptions.statement: If water looks clear and has no smell, it is safe to drink.
misconceptions.why: Clear water is associated with purity.
misconceptions.fix: Germs and some chemicals are invisible, so clear water may be unsafe. Boil, filter or chlorinate it if source is uncertain.

probe.question: Is clear river water safe to drink directly?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is clear so it is clean.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about water purity

misconceptions.statement: A filter or cloth removes all germs from water.
misconceptions.why: Filtering seems to remove everything unwanted.
misconceptions.fix: A cloth removes only large particles. Boiling or chlorination is needed to kill germs, unless a proper purifier is used.

probe.question: Does straining water through cloth make it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all germs are removed.

misconceptions.root_belief: separation works for all sizes

misconceptions.statement: Antibiotics cure colds and flu.
misconceptions.why: Antibiotics are called the medicine for infections.
misconceptions.fix: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only against bacteria. Use them only when a doctor prescribes.

probe.question: A child has flu. Will antibiotics cure it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, antibiotics kill the flu germs.

misconceptions.root_belief: one medicine treats all related things
misconceptions.source_hint: surveys of public understanding of antibiotics

misconceptions.statement: Stop antibiotics once you feel better.
misconceptions.why: Symptoms vanish before all germs are gone.
misconceptions.fix: Finish the full course the doctor prescribed. Stopping early can leave bacteria alive and help them become resistant.

probe.question: Fever is gone on day 2 of a 5-day course. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Stop taking the medicine.

misconceptions.root_belief: feeling better means problem is gone
misconceptions.source_hint: public health surveys on antibiotic use

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines give you the disease so they are unsafe.
misconceptions.why: Students hear that a vaccine contains the germ.
misconceptions.fix: Vaccines use weakened, killed or partial germs, so the body learns to defend without getting the disease.

probe.question: Does a vaccine give you the disease?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it injects the disease into you.

misconceptions.root_belief: the cause itself is what is given
